slides.title: What this session is about
slides.content: A couple of weeks in, you've started to find your feet. This module is about the things that decide how the rest of the year goes — how you organise yourself, how you build confidence in this new place, and yes, attendance. It's a ~60 minute teacher-led session and there's nothing to revise.

slides.title: The session in six beats
slides.content: There are six beats in today's session: (1) What changes from school, (2) Time and organisation, (3) Seek Opportunity, (4) Confidence, (5) Attendance, (6) Your habit. Three threads — transition, organisation, attendance — and one commitment activity at the end.

exercise.explanation: All of these are covered in the section on The Shift from School to College.

slides.title: What's actually different — school → college
slides.content: Three honest contrasts. At school, someone chased you when work was missing — at college, no one chases; the work is yours, or it doesn't get done. At school, your day was filled in for you — at college, you have big chunks of unstructured time and you decide what they're for. At school, a bad week showed up next week — at college, a bad week shows up two months from now, quieter — and worse.

exercise.explanation: The deck says: 'No one chases. The work is yours — or it doesn't get done.'

slides.title: The long fuse — where consequences actually land
slides.content: Most missed work doesn't punish you that week. It punishes you a couple of months later, when you can't catch up — and you didn't know you needed to. That's the actual time-management problem. The one move that actually helps is to treat your unstructured periods as actual sessions — a specific thing, for a specific lesson, for a set amount of time. The students who do this don't work harder than everyone else. They just decide in advance.

slides.title: Seek Opportunity — what independence actually looks like
slides.content: Seek Opportunity is the honest version of 'be independent'. Three concrete behaviours: (1) Join clubs and volunteer when you can — enter a short film or digital media competition, build a public portfolio on Behance or Vimeo, or apply for a student media or journalism project at the college. (2) Explore careers and build your skills — research BA degrees at University Centre Hastings, digital media and film degrees, and Higher Apprenticeship routes in software development, cybersecurity or content production. The UK games industry alone is worth almost £4 billion. (3) Treat mistakes as how you learn — not the embarrassing bit, the useful bit.

slides.title: What confidence actually is
slides.content: Most students feel out of depth in their first weeks at college — not some, most. It's a sign you've moved up, not that you're in the wrong place. Confidence isn't a personality trait — it's what you build by doing things you weren't sure you could. The trap is: 'I'm finding this hard, so I must not be cut out for it.' The honest version is: 'I'm finding this hard. That means I'm doing it properly — and I should ask.'

slides.title: Attendance — the plain case
slides.content: There's no percentage threshold and no threats in this deck. The plain case is what you genuinely lose when you're not in the room: (1) the bit that isn't on the slides — off-script teaching, worked examples, questions answered live; (2) spaced learning that actually sticks — knowledge built across weeks beats knowledge crammed in a fortnight; (3) the relationships that catch you when you slip — teachers who know you, classmates who notice you're missing; (4) being seen — by the people writing your reference.

slides.title: When coming in is hard
slides.content: Attendance isn't always about willpower. Real barriers include: mental health (anxiety, low mood, sleep that doesn't come); money and travel (when bus fares add up); things at home (caring responsibilities, family pressure, unsafe situations); neurodivergence not yet supported, or chronic health; friendships or feeling like you don't fit — bigger than people admit. The key line: a barrier we know about is one we can help with. A barrier we don't know about is one that quietly takes you out. Tell someone. Early.

exercise.explanation: A barrier we know about is one we can help with. Tell someone. Early.

slides.title: Your one habit for this week
slides.content: Habits change behaviour. Plans don't. Pick ONE specific thing you'll do this week — not five. The four options on the card are drawn from the deck: (a) decide in advance what one free period is for; (b) ask for help with the thing you've been quietly stuck on; (c) do one Seek-Opportunity thing — a club, a careers event, asking a question; (d) tell someone about a barrier that's making attendance hard.
